body:
Extract 2D nesting outlines from 3D models (`STEP`, `STL`, `OBJ`, and `.sc` `#1456`) and instance 2.5D/3D operations at each placed part on a router sheet.

Depends on #2158, #2160, and #2161.

## Scope

- **3D orientation and sheet-face selection (`crates/app/`, `crates/geometry/`):**
  - Allow a user to pick a planar face (`FeatureSel::Face` or `FeatureSel::Patch`) on a 3D model to lie flat on the sheet (`normal -> -Z`), or default to the model's current `-Z` base face (`z_min` seated at `z = 0`).
  - Store the chosen sheet-face orientation on the `NestPart` entry (undoable command parameter).
- **2D silhouette extraction and thickness checks (`crates/geometry/src/geometry/slice.rs`):**
  - Project the oriented 3D mesh along the sheet normal via `slice::project` (`crates/geometry/src/geometry/slice.rs`) to obtain the outer loop and through-holes (`Region`).
  - Measure model height `z_max - z_min`. Refuse by model name when `model_height > sheet_thickness` within tolerance.
- **Flat-extrusion check vs 2.5D/3D router instancing:**
  - Compare `slice::at_z` cross-sections at bottom, mid, and top planes against `slice::project` to detect non-flat features (pockets, blind holes, steps, chamfers).
  - On pure 2D through-cut nests (`Kind::Waterjet`, `Kind::Plasma`), refuse non-flat 3D parts by name unless the user explicitly enables `outline_only`.
  - On `Kind::Mill` (CNC router) nests, nest using the full outer XY silhouette plus cutter diameter and gap, then replicate the part's authored 2.5D/3D operations (`Pocket`, `Drill`, `Chamfer2D`, `Contour`, `Pocket3D`) transformed to each placed instance `(tx, ty, angle_deg)` on the sheet setup.
  - Sequence all internal 2.5D/3D operations across all placed instances before outer `Contour` cutout passes so hold-down stays intact.

## Done means

Tests load a 3D `STEP`/`STL` bracket and a pocketed 2.5D plate, orient a chosen face onto the sheet, refuse parts taller than the sheet thickness by name, refuse non-flat parts on waterjet/plasma unless `outline_only` is set, and nest plus generate transformed 2.5D router toolpaths on every placed instance with outer cutouts running last.

body:
Extend the 2D nesting engine and document/UI model with deterministic fixed-budget local search, irregular remnant sheet support, and waste-outline export.

Depends on #2158, #2160, and #2163.

## Sources and clean room

- Gomes and Oliveira, *A 2-exchange heuristic for nesting problems*, EJOR 2002.
- Reuse `crates/geometry/src/geo2d.rs` (`Region::difference`, `Region::offset_sharp`, `Region::bounds`).
- Do not read or adapt external nesting implementations (SVGnest, Deepnest, WAM, Fusion, HSMWorks).

## Scope

- **Deterministic local-search packing (`crates/geometry/src/nesting/`):**
  - Add an optional `Optimize` mode using deterministic 2-exchange swaps and rotation perturbations over the BLF placement order.
  - Bound search work by a fixed evaluation budget (`max_evals`), never a wall-clock timeout, so repeated runs always return the exact same layout.
- **Remnant sheet and keep-out zones (`crates/geometry/`, `crates/app/`, `crates/ui/`):**
  - Allow a sheet definition to include an irregular outer boundary (from a DXF/SVG remnant outline or a previous nest waste region) and internal cutout holes or clamp keep-out zones.
  - Ensure NFP/IFP checks keep all placed part kerfs inside the usable remnant and outside every keep-out hole.
- **Waste outline and remnant export:**
  - Compute the unconsumed sheet remnant `Region` (`sheet_region.difference(&union_of_kerf_footprints)`) and largest guillotine leftover strip.
  - Add an export action (DXF/SVG or reusable `Sketch` remnant) and UI overlay toggle for the waste outline.

## Done means

Tests verify deterministic local search matches or improves single-pass BLF utilization across identical inputs, remnant sheet tests place parts cleanly around pre-existing sheet holes and keep-outs, and the unconsumed waste `Region` exports and reloads as a remnant sheet cleanly.

body:
Add a global sheet cut-order tree, hold-down sequencing, and cut-side planner in `crates/geometry/src/nesting/` (reusing the nesting rules from `crates/motion/src/plasma/nest.rs`).

Depends on #2158 and #1861.

## Scope

- Build one global containment forest across all closed contours and open chains on a nested sheet.
- Assign each open chain to its smallest enclosing closed contour, or mark it top-level when outside all parts.
- Assign each contour and chain a resolved cut role and cut side:
  - Closed loops: `Outside`, `OnLine`, or `Inside` (`Auto` sets outer part outlines to `Outside`, holes to `Inside`, and islands inside holes to `Outside`).
  - Open chains: `OnLine`, `Left`, or `Right`.
  - Refuse `Inside` or `Outside` on an open chain by name.
- Traverse the global containment tree in deterministic iterative post-order:
  - Cut internal holes, pockets, and open features of a part before its outer outline.
  - Cut small parts nested inside a hole before the enclosing hole cuts free.
  - Order sibling parts at the same depth by increasing area (small parts before large parts) to preserve router vacuum hold-down and sheet rigidity.
  - Reserve ordered pass phases: marking/scribe passes (`#1447`) first, internal/pocket passes next, rough/onion-skin profile passes next, and final onion-skin breakthrough passes last.
- Compute minimum inside-corner cutter-radius clearance diagnostics when a circular tool (`radius = cut_width / 2`) cannot reach sharp concave corners.
- Validate that no contour cuts after an enclosing contour has already freed its material.

## Done means

Tests in `crates/geometry` verify inside-out cut order across a multi-part sheet containing nested holes, internal open cuts, and a small part placed inside a large hole, verify phase ordering for marking and onion-skin passes, confirm smaller sibling parts precede larger ones deterministically, report concave inside-corner radius limits, and refuse invalid open-chain side requests by name.

body:
Add a deterministic 2D true-shape nesting kernel in `crates/geometry/src/nesting/` (no ECS, no world).

## Sources and clean room

Write this module from published literature and CamCraft code only:
- Bennell and Oliveira, *The geometry of nesting problems: a tutorial*, EJOR 2008.
- Burke, Hellier, Kendall, and Whitwell, *A new bottom-left-fill heuristic algorithm for the two-dimensional irregular packing problem*, Operations Research 2006.
- Burke, Hellier, Kendall, and Whitwell, *Complete and robust no-fit polygon generation for the irregular stock cutting problem*, EJOR 2007.
- Reuse `crates/geometry/src/geo2d.rs` (`Region`, `Loop`, `Point2`, `Region::offset_sharp`) and `crates/geometry/src/geo2d/sweep.rs` (`Region::sweep`).
- Do not read or adapt code from HSMWorks, Autodesk Fusion, WAM, SVGnest, or Deepnest.

## Scope

- Define clean input and output structs in `crates/geometry/src/nesting/`:
  - Sheet input: width, height, `edge_margin`, `cut_width` (kerf or router cutter diameter), `part_gap`, and `allow_parts_in_holes`.
  - Part input: stable part id, quantity, outer loop, hole loops, optional open chains, default cut side (`Outside`, `OnLine`, `Inside`), `rotation_mode` (`Locked`, `Orthogonal`, `FixedStep(deg)`), and `allow_mirror`.
- Inflate each part before nesting so separate cuts keep at least `part_gap` of uncut material between cut edges:
  - Inflate `Outside` outer loops by `cut_width + part_gap / 2`.
  - Inflate `OnLine` outer loops by `cut_width / 2 + part_gap / 2`.
  - Inflate `Inside` outer loops by `part_gap / 2`.
  - Buffer standalone open chains via `Region::sweep` (`cut_width / 2 + part_gap / 2` for `OnLine`, `cut_width + part_gap / 2` for side cuts).
  - Support router single-slot clearance mode (`part_gap >= cut_width`) when adjacent outside profiles share a single cutter-width channel.
- Shrink the usable sheet inward by `edge_margin` (plus outer `cut_width` clearance) via `Region::offset_sharp`.
- Compute No-Fit Polygons (NFP) and Inner-Fit Polygons (IFP) on the `geo2d::SCALE` (1-micron) grid.
- Place parts with deterministic Bottom-Left-Fill (BLF):
  - Sort parts by decreasing area first. Break ties by part id and instance index.
  - Try candidate rotations (and mirroring only when `allow_mirror` is true).
  - Place small parts inside usable closed holes (`IFP(hole_usable, part_inflated)`) when `allow_parts_in_holes` is true.
  - Open new sheets when parts do not fit on active sheets.
- Report `sheet_count`, per-sheet placed counts per part (`placed_counts`), total placed vs requested quantities, per-sheet and overall `utilization_pct` (`sum(part_net_area) / sheet_area * 100.0`), `waste_region` (`sheet_region.difference(&union_of_cut_footprints)`), used sheet bounds, and an explicit `unplaced` list with refusal reasons.
- Add the one-line provenance comment at the module head.

## Done means

Unit tests in `crates/geometry` nest irregular parts, parts with holes, and swept open chains deterministically across 1 and multiple sheets, report exact per-sheet part counts and `utilization_pct`, place a small part inside a large part hole with full clearance, confirm zero overlap among inflated footprints, verify waste `Region`, and refuse non-finite, negative, or oversized inputs by name.

body:
Asked for by the user (2026-11-16, in chat), after comparing CamCraft with WAZER's WAM software, which "requires closed paths" and "does not do nesting":

> "By nesting, I mean here are parts, figure out how to optimally place them so I can minimize material waste"

> "I'd suspect the workflow would be to open the models (probably svg and dxf files, enter material info (dimensions, type, thickness), kerf and minimal space between cuts, and you'd press a button to have it do layout. WAM had options to do inside, on line, or outside line cutting. The cutting logic gets tricky because you have to do some cuts (like internal features) first"

## What is missing

CamCraft has no automatic nesting: there is no way to give it a set of 2D parts and a sheet and have it place the parts to waste as little material as possible. `#1447` (common-line cutting in a nest) assumes the parts are already placed.

## Wanted workflow (from the user)

1. Open the part drawings: SVG (`#1880`) and DXF (`#1452`, `#1865`), several files, with a quantity per part.
2. Enter the sheet: width x height, material type, thickness.
3. Enter the kerf and the minimum gap between cuts (and from the sheet edge).
4. Choose the cut side per part or per profile: inside, on the line, or outside the line.
5. Press one button: CamCraft lays out the parts on the sheet (and on more sheets if they do not fit), and shows the use of material.
6. The cut order follows from the layout: internal features (holes) before the part outline, small parts before the parts around them, and no part cut free while a later cut still needs it.

## Open questions (research)

1. **Algorithm.** True-shape nesting from published literature, for example no-fit polygons (Bennell and Oliveira, "The geometry of nesting problems: a tutorial", EJOR 2008; Burke et al., "Complete and robust no-fit polygon generation for the irregular stock cutting problem", EJOR 2007) with a bottom-left fill or a local-search placement order. Which method, what run time is acceptable, and is the result deterministic (same input, same layout)?
2. **Rotations and mirroring.** Free rotation, fixed steps (0/90/180/270 or 15 degrees), or locked (grain direction, a printed face)? Mirroring allowed?
3. **Spacing.** How the kerf, the minimum gap, leads and pierce points enter the spacing (offset each part by half the kerf plus half the gap before nesting?). The sheet edge margin, and holes or scrap areas already in the sheet (a remnant).
4. **Parts in holes.** May a small part be placed inside a large part's hole?
5. **Document model.** Is a nest a new entity (sheet + placed part instances) with undoable commands (`CreateNest`, `EditNest`, `RunNesting`) and their MCP tools (AGENTS.md "Everything Is a Command" and "Commands ship with an MCP tool")? How does it relate to setups and stock?
6. **Cut order.** Holes before outlines; inside-out for parts inside holes; the "no part drops before its remaining cuts" rule shared with `#1447`; which machine kinds (waterjet, plasma, laser, router sheet jobs).
7. **Cut side.** Inside / on / outside the line per profile, mapped onto the 2D profile and waterjet operations (`#1883`), with open paths handled where the operation allows (WAM cannot cut open paths).
8. **Output.** Material use (percent), the waste outline, and a sheet count.

## Clean room

Specify from published literature and our own design notes only. Do not read or adapt nesting code or other CAM programs' internals (Fusion, HSMWorks, WAM's JavaScript, SVGnest, Deepnest and the like are not sources). The user's own WAM projects (G-code beside `.wzr` files, which the user cleared for reading) may be used only to compare CamCraft's output on the same parts.

## Done means

The open questions are answered in comments on this issue, and the concrete sub-issues are filed (each with one `P*`, one `effort:*`, `area:*`, `source:agent`, a "Done means" line and "Part of #N"), linked back here; then `needs-research` is dropped and this umbrella closes.

Related: `#1447` (common-line cutting in a nest), `#1883` (waterjet profile operation), `#1886` (WAZER machines and post), `#1880` (SVG import), `#1452` (DXF import), `#1861` (outer vs hole chaining).

body:
What happens: PR #2138's re-read `acquit_traverses_by_prior` (crates/sim/src/verify/prior_traverse.rs) acquits a convicted rapid at the clearance plane when what the program ahead left standing is under the tip. Its stated law treats "outside what the map models" two ways: a capsule part that falls off the stock grid is clamped away and reads as air (module doc: "off the grid is outside the stock (air)"), while a column whose height is not a number reads as unknown, and unknown is never proof of air (module doc, line 23, and the #1056 fidelity law). The doc backs the first reading with a condition: the solid law shares the conviction, and an off-grid part "must not be acquitted with the column's".

title: Tilted plane (3+2): a Tool axis A of 180 degrees is refused with no reason, and the plane of the A0 B180 face has X and Y exchanged

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: area:multiaxis
labels.description: 3+2, 5-axis, rotary

labels.name: area:ui
labels.description: User interface and picking

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Wrong behaviour a user hits, with a workaround; fix now

body:
Found during the work on #1904 ("Your first 4-axis part", Tormach 770MX + microARC 4), on `main` at `af83da0f4`.

A 4th-axis table about X can turn the part to A180. `tormach.cps` posts that index as `G0 A180`, and `the_canonical_b180_pose_posts_as_a180` pins it. But the operation page does not let the user ask for it directly.

## 1. A Tool axis A of 180 is refused, and the refusal gives no reason

Steps:
1. Mount `Tormach 770MX + microARC 4`. Add a tool and a box stock.
2. Add a Slot. On the Heights tab, tick **Tilted plane (3+2)**. Set **Tool axis A** to 180 and **Tool axis B** to 0. Choose **Apply**.

Result: the edit is refused with this text: `operation parameters are not usable for a Slot operation`. The MCP tool gives the same text: `add_operation: invalid parameters: operation parameters are not usable for a Slot operation`.

The cause is `Tilt::is_sane` in `crates/app/src/operation/types/params.rs`. It accepts A from -90 to 90 and B from -180 to 180. The pose law writes the face opposite the top as A 0, B 180. The refusal does not name the tilt, the limits, or the A 0 B 180 pose. A microARC 4 user thinks in A only, and cannot find the remedy from this text.

The workaround is to type A 0 and B 180. The guide page for #1904 documents it.

## 2. The plane of the A 0 B 180 face has X and Y exchanged

`TiltedFrame::new` (`crates/cl/src/cl/frame.rs`) selects the in-plane axes from the smallest component of the tool axis. For A 90 and A -90, plane X is machine X (the rotary axis). For A 0 B 180, `sin(180 degrees)` is not exactly zero, the seed becomes Y, and plane X is machine Y and plane Y is machine X.

Result: the same flat along the bar has the ends (-0.75, 0) and (-0.25, 0) on three faces, but (0, -0.75) and (0, -0.25) on the fourth face. The page does not show the plane axes, so the user finds this only from the toolpath preview.

The posted program is correct in each case. The post reads the tool tip in machine coordinates.

## Proposed change

- Refuse an out-of-range tilt by name. Give the limits, and say that the face opposite the top is A 0 B 180.
- Or accept A beyond 90 degrees at the door and store the canonical pose.
- For a pose with no X component of the tool axis, keep plane X on machine X. Or show the plane X and Y directions on the page.

A change to the frame basis changes the paths of existing A 0 B 180 operations. Thus this work is under the safety floor.

Done means: a user who types Tool axis A = 180 on an A-table machine gets the A180 index or a refusal that names the remedy. The plane X of the A 0 B 180 face is on the rotary axis, or the page shows the plane axes. A test pins each item. The guide page `first-4axis-part.md` is updated.

Refs #1904, #797.

body:
Found while working #1559 (issue-worker-high, upstream main ce59ef446).

## What happens

The rapid law convicts "rapid move N travels below the clearance plane inside stock" - a rapid **at** the clearance plane is never judged. So when the clearance plane itself is set inside the stock (a Fixed height, or Top-of-Model + an offset smaller than the stock allowance), the op's traverse runs through uncut stock and the program **posts with no warning**.

Reproduced headlessly (synthetic fixture of `crates/app/tests/top_stock.rs`):

- Stock box 40 x 40 x 10 (top Z10), part a 10 x 10 x 5 cube at the origin.
- 2D Contour on the part, `clearance_z = Fixed 8`, `retract_z = Fixed 8`, Top 5, Bottom 0, stepdown 2.5, Plunge entry.
- Generated path: move 0 `Rapid (0,0,8) -> (10.35,-2.98,8)` - a lateral rapid 2 mm under the stock top, through the stock; the machine also arrives at Z8 over (0,0), inside the stock column.
- `tp.warnings == []`, and `posting::post_setup_unwritten` returns `Ok`.

Nothing at command creation refuses a clearance below the stock top either (Contour validation only checks clearance >= Top, retract >= Top).

## Why P1

A rapid through uncut stock is a collision that passes (AGENTS.md P1: "a gouge or collision that passes"). The default heights reference the stock top, so a user has to set the plane low, but a Fixed or model-referenced clearance on a taller stock is ordinary input.

## Done means

- A rapid at (not only under) the clearance plane that passes through stock the program ahead has not removed is convicted (`RapidInStock` or a named clearance-in-stock warning) and holds the post - or a clearance/retract plane under the remaining stock top over the op's travel is refused by name at generation.
- Pinned by a test for the repro above (Contour) and one other ladder kind; the #96/#1066/#1091 rapid-law pins unchanged.

body:
Part of #1490. Found while working #2031 (the motion-crate generator `camcraft_motion::machining2d::rest_adaptive`).

What happens: the rest Adaptive planner keeps a pass only when its whole feed reads at most the optimal load (plus the plain Adaptive's 5% planning margin) on the remaining stock. Two shapes cannot be cut under that rule, and the whole operation is then refused by name ("rest Adaptive cannot hold the optimal load at (x, y), Z...: ... choose Waterline or Offset rings"):

- A pocket corner where the cutter's center has to turn on a tight arc (a square CAD corner is the extreme). The last sliver wraps about a quarter of the cutter however thin it is: the contact angle does not fall with the depth of cut. Measured with a 4 mm tool after a 12 mm tool: a center arc of 1.0 mm (3 mm pocket fillet) and of 1.2 mm (3.5 mm fillet, 0.3 mm left on the walls) is cut; 0.7 mm (3 mm fillet, 0.3 mm left) is refused; on a 60 x 40 pocket with square corners the sharp phase reads 56.5 degrees against 47.5 and 9.6% of the rest material is left, which is over the 2% coverage bound, so it is refused.
- A neck under about 2.5 tool diameters wide. A 10 mm neck is cut by a 4 mm tool in half loops (128 passes a depth); a 6 mm neck is refused.

Both are pinned as refusals in `crates/motion/tests/rest_adaptive/main.rs` (`a_pocket_corner_too_sharp_to_turn_in_within_the_load_is_refused_by_name`, `a_neck_too_narrow_to_hold_the_load_is_refused_by_name`).

What needs deciding (the maintainer's call), then building:

1. Sharp corners: (a) keep the refusal; (b) leave the corner rest standing and say so in a note with its area and place, the way the plain Adaptive leaves corner rest for a finishing pass; (c) cut it over the load up to a named cap. Today (b) happens only when the rest left is under 2% of the rest material in reach.
2. Narrow necks: a trochoidal plan with its own step law (the plain Adaptive has one, `adaptive/troch_plan.rs`, built for a whole center area and its own entry), or keep the refusal.

Literature to start from: M. Otkur and I. Lazoglu, "Trochoidal milling", Int. J. Machine Tools and Manufacture 47, 2007; J. A. Stori and P. K. Wright, "Constant engagement tool path generation for convex geometries", J. Manufacturing Systems 19(3), 2000. No other CAM product's code or output (Clean-Room Protocol).

Done means: the decision for each of the two shapes is recorded in `docs/decisions/`; the chosen behaviour is built with its pinning tests (verifier clean, no rapid or plunge into material, the load measured on a simulated stock, any rest left named), or the refusal is confirmed and its wording says what the user can do.

The `camcraft-ui` program reads start options, but `--help` does not show them. The user cannot find them without the source.

The options that the source reads (`crates/ui/src/egui_app/mod.rs`, `crates/ui/src/egui_app/gpu.rs`, `crates/ui/src/lib.rs`):

- `--gpu-backend <name>` and the variable `CAMCRAFT_GPU_BACKEND`
- `--gpu <adapter name>` and the variable `CAMCRAFT_GPU`
- the MCP port option and the variable `CAMCRAFT_MCP_PORT`
- `--headless`
- `--ui`

The worker must find each option and each variable that the program reads. This list can be incomplete.

2. `--help` and `-h` print the help text and exit before a window or a GPU device is made.
3. `--version` prints the version and exits.
4. An option that the program does not know gives a clean error that names it and points to `--help`. The program does not start with a wrong option ignored.
5. Write the help text in plain English (no G-code terms).
6. Add the options to the user guide page that describes how to start the program.

body:
The maintainer reported this in chat on 2026-11-16. His words: "its just to much compile in each "batch".. so it takes forever to get thru a post-merge-gate - even with -j6 set.. if u set a -j6.. there should be 2 cores per procss. so a max of 3 tests per batch.."

## What happens

- `xtask/src/plan.rs` gives each cargo step `-j 6` and `--test-threads=6` (`J`, `T`).
- `xtask/src/lanes.rs` runs up to `LIMIT = 4` steps at the same time in the release tier.
- Each lane keeps the full `-j 6` and `--test-threads=6`. Four lanes thus start up to 24 compile jobs and 24 test threads.
- The gate also shares its machine with review builds and worker builds. Each of those uses `-j 6` too.
- The result is more jobs than cores. Each lane is slower than a serial run.

## What to do

1. Make the job count one budget for the whole gate (default 6). Read it from one constant, with an environment override.
2. When N lanes run at the same time, give each lane `-j (budget / N)` and `--test-threads=(budget / N)`, minimum 1.
3. Set the lane limit from the budget: at most `budget / 2` lanes. With a budget of 6 this is 3 lanes with 2 jobs each.
4. A step that runs alone keeps the full budget.
5. Print the budget, the lane count and the jobs for each lane at the start of the gate.
6. Apply the same rule to each tier that runs lanes, and to #1941 if it adds lanes to the quick and batch tiers.
7. Update the `gate` skill and the `runners` skill: the sum of `-j` of all builds on one machine stays at or below its core count.

## Done means

- A unit test in `xtask` shows that the sum of `-j` in each wave is at or below the budget, and that no wave has more than `budget / 2` lanes.
- A unit test shows that a step that runs alone gets the full budget.
- `cargo xtask gate release --dry-run` prints the budget and the jobs for each lane.
- The PR body has the wall time of one batch run and one release wave, before and after.
- The PR body has the line `Process change: yes`.

body:
The maintainer asked for this in chat on 2026-11-15. His words: "Issue, on Geometry tabs, under Boundaries.. there should be selection for faces and edges that is "do not touch".. and he calculation should avoid to gouge them at all costs."

## What is missing

An operation has no way to name model faces or edges that the tool must not touch. The user cannot protect a finished surface, a datum face or a sharp edge from a later operation.

## What to do

1. Add a "Do not touch" selection to the Boundaries group of the Geometry tab of an operation.
   - The user picks faces and edges in the viewport.
   - Each picked item shows as a row with a remove button.
   - The viewport shows the protected items in a different colour while the operation is selected.
2. Store the selection on the operation. The change goes through an undoable command (AGENTS.md "Everything Is a Command"). The command ships with its MCP tool.
3. Add a clearance parameter (default 0, the stock to leave still applies). The tool stays this distance from each protected item.
4. Each generator that the operation type uses keeps the tool clear of the protected items. This includes the cutting moves, the lead moves, the link moves and the plunges. The check uses the full tool: flutes, shank and holder.
5. The verify gate checks each generated move against the protected items. This check is independent of the generator.
6. If a move touches a protected item, the operation is refused or marked "incomplete" with a diagnostic that names the item. The post is blocked. The program is never posted with such a move (AGENTS.md "Prime Directive: Never Crash, Never Gouge").
7. If a protected item is also in the machining selection of the same operation, refuse the selection when the command is created. Say which item is in the two lists.
8. The project file stores the selection. Say in the PR if older builds refuse the new file.

## Scope

- First slice: the selection, the command, the MCP tool, the verify check and the refusal, for one 2D and one 3D operation type. The PR names the two types.
- Later slices: the other operation types. File one issue for each family (2D, 3D, multi-axis, turning, wire).
- Reference material is public machining literature and published user documentation at behaviour level only (AGENTS.md "Clean-Room Protocol"). Write the labels in our own words.

## Safety

This work is under the safety floor. It adds a gouge law and can change posted G-code for an operation that has protected items. An operation without protected items must give the same toolpath as before: pin that.

## Done means

- The Geometry tab has the "Do not touch" selection under Boundaries, with pick, list and remove.
- Undo and redo restore the selection. The MCP tool sets and reads it.
- A test with a protected face next to the cut region shows that no move comes nearer than the clearance.
- A test with a protected face that the selected region cannot avoid shows the refusal, with the item named, and a blocked post.
- A test shows that an operation without protected items gives a toolpath that does not change.
- The structural UI test asserts the new rows and their labels.
- The user guide describes the selection and the refusal.

body:
Part of #1490.

The rest generator currently trusts an entered previous tool. It assumes that tool cut the pocket to the requested depth.

Add a previous-operations mode that derives remaining material from the stock those operations actually leave.

Design decision:
- Keep the entered-tool mode explicit. Add a separate previous-operations mode through an undoable command, the project file, and MCP.
- Read only earlier operations in the same setup, in their actual order. Reuse the established carried-stock infrastructure.
- Require current operation paths and compatible setup coordinates. Refuse missing, stale, or unsupported stock by name, or mark the result incomplete.
- Read remaining stock at every requested cut depth. A shallow roughing pass does not prove that the lower floor is clear.
- Include tool shape, wall and floor allowances, and the supported simulation resolution. Unknown cells remain occupied.
- Pass a conservative remaining-material region to the motion generator. Do not infer cleared volume from the previous tool diameter alone.
- Invalidate the result when an earlier operation changes, moves, is suppressed, or changes its tool or depth.
- Keep the current stock backend. Do not combine this feature with the field-engine migration in #586 or #637.

Tests:
- Compare the rest region with independently simulated earlier operations.
- Test mixed previous tool sizes, bull-nose tools, partial depths, wall allowances, islands, and disconnected cuts.
- Test missing paths, stale paths, operation reordering, changed tools, and unsupported stock frames.
- Prove the plan never removes material from its rest estimate unless the earlier cuts prove that material absent.
- Prove command undo, project save and reopen, MCP editing, and dependency invalidation.
- Remove each depth and stock-validity guard separately. Each mutation must fail its pinning test.

Done means: previous-operations mode uses conservative stock at each depth, passes these tests, and never guesses when stock cannot be established.

Related: #586 and #637 migrate the stock representation. This issue consumes the current representation for 2D rest machining.

Literature: M. Held, On the Computational Geometry of Pocket Machining, LNCS 500 (1991), https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/3-540-54103-9. Z. Yao, S. K. Gupta and D. S. Nau, Algorithms for selecting cutters in multi-part milling problems, Computer-Aided Design 35 (2003), https://www.cs.umd.edu/~nau/papers/yao2003algorithms.pdf.

These sources describe pocket geometry and cutter coverage. The per-depth stock and invalidation contract above is this project's decision. Do not copy another CAM product's code or output.

The current rest pass plunges at each rest area. PR #1817 measures two corner entries per level that touch rest material at the cutter rim.

- Use conservative stock from the previous operations at the entry's actual depth.
- Prove clearance for the full cutter footprint throughout the descent and the lateral approach.
- Do not accept a clear tool axis as proof of a clear cutter rim.
- Keep unknown stock occupied. Account for simulation resolution and tool geometry in the clearance margin.
- Keep the approach inside the legal cutter-center region. Check islands, walls, stock, fixtures, and the supported tool envelope.
- Refuse the requested cleared-space entry by name when no proved route exists. Do not silently use an assumed entry hole.
- Keep ordinary cutting entry available as an explicit separate choice. Do not change its behavior as part of this task.

- Require the full cutter footprint to remain clear during descent. Measure stock contact during the lateral cutting feed separately.
- Test shallow roughing, a bull-nose previous tool, islands, disconnected cleared regions, and insufficient entry room.
- Require named refusals for missing or stale stock and unsupported depth.
- Remove each footprint, depth, and stock-validity guard separately. Each mutation must fail its pinning test.

Done means: the fixture enters without plunging its rim into rest material, passes verification, and refuses every unproved entry case by name.

Related: #1816 reduces air cutting on the inner legs of corner rings. This issue changes the entry, not those ring legs.

body:
The maintainer reported this in chat on 2026-11-15, on v0.21.0, with a screenshot of a 2D Adaptive operation.

His words: "a common issue i see is that the first toolpath is always ontop of the part at TopZ ... even thos stepdown states "full depth" of the cut.. technically it should just be one single toolpath right?" and "find it in all operations.. This is a high effortf, P2 bug.."

## What happens

The operation has Top Z = 13 (stock top + 1), Bottom Z = 0 and Stepdown = 50 mm. It posts two full levels: one at Z 13 and one at Z 0. The level at Top Z cuts no material. It doubles the cycle time of a one-level cut.

## Cause

The shared level law starts its list at Top Z:

```rust
// crates/motion/src/machining2d/levels.rs, cut_levels
let mut z = top;
while z > bottom + tol {
    zs.push(z);      // the first level is `top`
    z -= stepdown;
}
zs.push(bottom);
```

`cut_levels(13, 0, 50)` gives `[13, 0]`. The correct list is `[0]`. With a stepdown of 5 it gives `[13, 8, 3, 0]`. The correct list is `[8, 3, 0]`.

`crates/app/src/operation/area.rs` `ladder_planes` restates the same law, and its unit test pins the wrong list (`ladder_planes(20.0, 0.0, 5.0) == [20, 15, 10, 5, 0]`).

## Callers found (read-only search, not complete)

- `crates/motion/src/machining2d/`: `adaptive_troch.rs:158`, `bore.rs:308`, `circular.rs:278` and `:280`, `contour_params.rs:216` (2D Contour), `face.rs:156`, `pocket.rs:277`, `pocket_hsm.rs:49` and `pocket_troch.rs:68` (level counts for the budget), `slots.rs:160` and `:343`, `trochoid_slot.rs:319`
- `crates/motion/src/machining3d/entry.rs:89`, `:123`, `:236`, `:258` (3D Pocket and its rest pass)
- `crates/app/src/operation/area.rs:74`, `:182`, `:233` (`ladder_planes`, the 3D pocket region build)
- `crates/motion/tests/control_comp.rs` (a test helper with the same name)

Not yet read: `crates/motion/src/finishing3d/ladder.rs` `levels`, `crates/motion/src/machining2d/contour_depth.rs` `ladder`, `crates/motion/src/machining3d/ladder.rs`, the turning, drilling (peck), engraving, chamfer, plasma and EDM depth ladders, and each operation with its own loop.

## For the work

1. Audit each operation of each machine type for a level at Top Z (or at the material top) that removes no material. List each in the PR with the result.
2. Fix the shared law so that the first level is `top - stepdown`, and the last level is `bottom` exactly. Use one law: `ladder_planes` in `app` must use the motion law, or match it by a shared test.
3. Check the special cases:
   - Top Z below the stock top (material above Top Z): no level may cut more than one stepdown. Find what each operation means by Top Z, and state it.
   - `circular.rs:278` starts at a previous level (`cut_levels(prev, floor, ...)`): make sure that it does not cut the previous level two times.
   - Face: a single pass at `cut_z` stays one pass.
   - A stepdown of 0 or a span of 0: the current refusal and the one-plane result stay.
   - Rest machining and the 3D Pocket shell levels: the level count and the budget readings change. Restate the budget pins with the reason.
   - The ramp, helix and plunge entries that read `top_z` as the material top (`Motion::top_z`) must stay correct.
4. The size of the last step (the remainder or equal steps) is a separate choice. Keep the current remainder rule, and file a follow-up issue for the choice.

This changes posted G-code for existing projects (one level fewer for each depth-stepping operation). It is under the safety floor.

## Done means

- No operation posts a level at Top Z that removes no material when Top Z is at or above the material top.
- One-level case: Top Z 13, Bottom Z 0, Stepdown 50 gives one level at Z 0. Pinned for 2D Adaptive, 2D Pocket, 2D Contour, Slot, Bore, Circular and 3D Pocket.
- Multi-level case: Top Z 20, Bottom Z 0, Stepdown 5 gives `[15, 10, 5, 0]`. Pinned on the shared law and on `ladder_planes`.
- Each changed golden is listed in the PR with the reason. The PR says that posted G-code changes.
- Each verify and gouge pin of the touched operations stays green.

- Define one explicit rotary sign convention (`table_rh` vs `tool_rh`) so the checker and post agree.
- Add optional `controller.rtcp` (boolean). When `false`, mirror `machine.rtcp = false` so `fanuc.cps` and `doosan-dnm.cps` refuse `G43.4`, and mirror the full rotary chain for CAM-side IK posts.
- Keep the unstated-limit rule from `assets/machines/AGENTS.md` and validate all new fields in `crates/app/src/machine/validate.rs`.

body:
Found during #1842.

## What happens

With "Threading: G76 cycle" and a flank infeed, the Fanuc lathe post writes one G76 cycle. Two published manuals show that the control ends every pass at the programmed end point D:

- FANUC Series 0i-F lathe operator's manual B-64604EN-1, section 4.2.7, Fig. 4.2.7 (a).
- Siemens SINUMERIK ISO Turning programming manual A5E52211627B, Fig. 4-25.

The turning kernel (`crates/motion/src/turning/thread.rs`, the pass loop) shifts the start AND the end of each pass by the same flank offset. Thus a shallower pass ends short of D by `(k - depth) * tan(a/2)`. Only the root pass ends at D.

## Effect

The control cuts each shallower pass a little longer than the laid pass that the verdict and the stock simulation see. The extra length is at a smaller depth, inside the groove that the root pass cuts to D. It removes no material beyond the root pass and does not move toward a shoulder. Thus this is not a wrong-output defect. But the simulated passes are not exactly the passes that run.

`crates/app/tests/lathe_post_g76_sources.rs::every_pass_runs_to_the_posted_end_z_inside_the_root_pass` pins the present difference.

## Done means

One of these:

- The kernel lays each flank pass of a G76-postable plan to the same end station, and the pin changes to assert that.
- Or a decision records why the present laid ends stay.

title: Mask tests: compare a generated toolpath with its described shape

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:2d
labels.description: 2D milling

labels.name: source:agent

labels.name: effort:max

labels.description: Accepted enhancement, not scheduled

body:
The maintainer asked for this in chat (2026-11-15):

> is it possible to use the cli tool to verify tool paths "visually".. we know what they should look like mathematically.. could we inspect them using rasterized tests?

> Idea is to sanity checks that changes to the motion crates actually gets implemented as described by the user

## Problem

A change to a toolpath generator is described in words in its issue (for example "the pass extends to the stock edge", "the corners are arcs", "the slot is cleared with trochoidal loops"). The tests of the change pin numbers that the author chose. No test compares the shape of the generated toolpath with the shape that the description gives. A change can pass its tests and not do what the user described.

## Proposal

Add a test helper that compares two masks on one grid:

- The expected region. The test builds it from the mathematical description (an outline, a depth, an extension).
- The swept region. The helper builds it from the tool footprint along the generated toolpath.

The helper gives these assertions:

- No overcut: no swept cell is outside the expected region, within one cell.
- Bounded leftover: the uncut area is below a stated limit, and the uncut cells are only in stated places.
- Engagement: no move cuts a width larger than the stated stepover.
- Shape laws: symmetry for a symmetric region, and no move outside the stock plus the stated extension.

When an assertion fails, the helper writes the difference mask as a PNG file into the test output folder. A person can then see where the toolpath is wrong. The test result comes from the numbers, not from an image comparison. No PNG golden is stored.

## Rules

- The helper is test code. It does not change a generator, a gouge check or a collision check.
- The helper is in the crate that owns the toolpath types (`crates/motion`), and uses the CPU rasteriser or its own grid. It does not need a GPU.
- The grid limits the precision to one cell. Exact laws (arc radius, depth, feed words) stay as numeric tests.
- A PR that changes a 2D generator in `crates/motion` adds or updates one mask test that states the described shape.

## First users

- Trochoidal slot.
- 2D Adaptive.
- The open-edge region of issue 1735 and the Slot extension of issue 1731.

Done means: the helper is in the repository with its own unit tests; the trochoidal slot and 2D Adaptive each have one mask test that fails when the generator is changed to overcut or to leave too much material (shown by a mutation check in the PR); a failed assertion writes the difference PNG; AGENTS.md "Testing" names the helper.

body:
Found while programming a simple 2.5D end-cap plate (user's project) with the CamCraft **v0.19.0** release CLI (macOS arm64), driven headlessly over MCP. Re-checked on upstream main **d00243a5**: **still reproduces, identical output**.

## What happens

Every 2D depth ladder cuts its first level at `top_z` (#514, kept by the maintainer on 2026-11-11). When Top is the faced material top, that level is a full pass in air. The obvious way to avoid it, setting Top to the first real cut, is **refused**: the entry rapids straight down to Top + the plunge height, which is inside the uncut stock above Top, and verify convicts it:

`rapid move 1 travels below the clearance plane inside stock`

So the air pass cannot be avoided. In the user's project the bore adaptive (2D Adaptive, three 0.25 in levels) keeps an air level at the faced top: **about 5.6 of its 16.9 min**.

Repro (main and v0.19.0 alike), a plate in stock 0.5 mm taller, faced to the part top first, `stepdown: 4`, bottom at the part bottom:

| op | `top_z` | levels (z) | first moves | verify |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2D Adaptive (bore) | TOS -0.5 (faced top) | 10 (air), 6, 2, 0 | rapid to z 12, feed down | ok |
| 2D Adaptive (bore) | TOS -4.5 | 6, 2, 0 | **rapid to z 8** (stock is at z 10) | `rapid move 1 travels below the clearance plane inside stock` |
| 2D Contour inside (bore) | TOS -0.5 | 10 (air), 6, 2, 0 | rapid to z 12, plunge | ok |
| 2D Contour inside (bore) | TOS -4.5 | 6, 2, 0 | **rapid to z 8** | same message, moves 1 and 5 |

The rapid law is right to convict a rapid into stock; the generator is what puts it there.

## Minimal repro (MCP)

`plate_bore.stl`: a 100 x 60 x 10 mm plate, centred, z 0..10, with a centred Ø40 through bore.

```
import_model   {"path": "plate_bore.stl", "name": "plate"}
add_setup      {"name": "Setup 1"}
set_stock      {"box": {"dx": 110, "dy": 70, "dz": 10.5}}
set_wcs        {"stock_point": {"x": "center", "y": "center", "z": "max"}}
add_tool       {"catalog": "EM-0600-4FL", "name": "EM6"}
add_operation  {"kind": "Face", "tool": "EM6", "name": "face", "params": {"cut_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -0.5}}}
add_operation  {"kind": "2D Adaptive", "tool": "EM6", "name": "op", "source": "plate",
                "params": {"top_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -4.5},
                           "bottom_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -10.5}, "stepdown": 4}}
set_operation_geometry {"operation": "op", "picks": [the bore's top chain]}
generate {} ; verify {}  -> "rapid move 1 travels below the clearance plane inside stock"
```

## Expected

An op whose Top is below the material standing over it enters safely: it rapids to the plunge height above the **material actually there** (the prior stock, or the stock top), then feeds (helix, ramp or plunge) down to its first level. `detect_holes` reports a through hole with `"floor_z"` at the part bottom and `"through": true`. - The 1.0 mm is not a parameter. It is not shown on the op, in the hole list or in `get_job`, and cannot be changed (the only way is to set `through: false` and type a deeper floor by hand, which is what the user did).
- It is not tied to anything under the part: not the stock bottom, a HAT web, the parallels or the setup. In the repro the part bottom is z 4.826 and the path goes to z 3.826 (the stock bottom is z 0). With the part bottom on the stock bottom, it cuts 1 mm below the stock, into whatever the part sits on, with no note (the fixture laws may catch a modelled parallel; an unmodelled table or spoilboard is not judged).
- It is in mm whatever the document units (an inch user would choose 0.020-0.040 in, and might want it scaled to the tool's tip, e.g. a drill's point length).

## Minimal repro (MCP)

```
import_model   {"path": "End Caps-End capSupport Plate.step", "name": "part"}
move_model     {"name": "part", "position": [0, 37.9, 4.826]}
add_setup      {"name": "Setup 1"}
set_stock      {"box": {"dx": 110, "dy": 185, "dz": 15.33}}
set_wcs        {"stock_point": {"x": "center", "y": "center", "z": "max"}}
add_tool       {"catalog": "EM-0400-2FL", "name": "EM4"}
add_operation  {"kind": "Bore", "tool": "EM4", "name": "Bore", "source": "part", "params": {"stepdown": 2.0}}
detect_holes   {"name": "Bore"}   -> every hole "floor_z": 4.826, "through": true
generate {}                       -> deepest feed z 3.826, no note
```

- The break-through is a visible, editable op parameter (default 1.0 mm or a tool-relative value), in document units, saved with the project and settable over MCP.
- The op says what it did (a note: "through holes run 1.0 mm past the part bottom, to z ...").
- The depth past the part is checked against what is under it: never below the stock bottom unless the user allows it, and refused by name if it would reach a fixture.

## Done means

- A through-hole break-through parameter on Drill, Bore and Thread (GUI field, project file, MCP `params`), with a default equal to today's 1.0 mm so existing goldens hold.
- The generated note states the break-through depth; a through hole whose break-through would go below the stock bottom is noted or refused; pinned by tests.

body:
Found while triaging issue 1510 (maintainer asked for a check against published references, 2026-11-13).

What we do today: a milling setup always cuts along the machine's Z as the model lies. The part is turned for a setup with Part alignment (issue 326). A WCS tilted off Z is refused at generation by name (PR 1518).

What the published documentation of the product we reimplement describes (behaviour only, read through a search summary, not verified page by page):
- The setup's WCS orientation sets the default tool direction: pointing the WCS Z out of another face makes that setup's 3-axis toolpaths cut from that direction; the model is not turned. The operator flips the part on the machine to match.
  - https://help.autodesk.com/cloudhelp/ENU/Fusion-CAM/files/MFG-TOOL-ORIENTATION-OVERVIEW.htm
  - https://www.autodesk.com/products/fusion-360/blog/fusion-360-wcs-tool-orientation/
- G54-G59 are translations on the machine (LinuxCNC also allows a rotation about Z); they do not re-aim the spindle: https://linuxcnc.org/docs/html/gcode/coordinates.html

So the reporter of 1510 used the workflow that documentation teaches. The maintainer's stated view (2026-11-13, in chat) is the opposite design: "You should orient the part to Z using Setup.. Not let the WCS orient the part to Z..". Both give the same posted program for a flipped part; they differ in which control the user turns.

To decide (maintainer):
1. Keep Part alignment as the only way to turn a part (today). Then the WCS pane should not offer a tilt for a milling setup, or should offer "turn the part with Part alignment" at that moment, so a user coming from the reference product is led there before Generate refuses.
2. Or let a tilted setup WCS define the tool direction (generate in the WCS frame; `docs/decisions/1510-tilted-wcs.md` rated that effort:max: every generator, stock, heights, simulation and the post's rotated-offset refusal are involved).

Safety: whichever is chosen, a tilted WCS never generates a path in a frame other than the one shown; the refusal of PR 1518 stays until option 2 is complete.

Done means: the maintainer's choice is recorded here; for option 1, the WCS pane change with its structural test; for option 2, sub-issues filed and this one closed as the umbrella.

title: Agent coordination broker: leases, heartbeats and dispatch across concurrent agents (coor CLI + Cloudflare Worker)

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:build
labels.description: Build, CI, release, tests

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.description: Large idea with open questions: research and file sub-issues before any code

labels.name: P?
labels.description: Paused: never picked until the maintainer sets a real priority

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
A proposal from a contributor (relayed by the user, 2026-11-13), with M5's assessment. Filed as research: open design questions to answer and break into sub-issues before any code.

## Problem

Several concurrent agents (Claude sessions on different subscriptions and machines, Codex, human contributors) work this repo. Today they coordinate only through GitHub text conventions:
- claim comments, re-read 60 s later for races;
- the 4 h agent and 48 h contributor staleness rules;
- `in-review`, `conflicts` and `merge-ready` labels;
- review markers;
- a review lock that is a local file on one machine;
- across subscriptions, messages are relayed by hand by the user.

The results are clashing PRs, stale claims, duplicated work (e.g. #1377 / #1379), and a human in the loop for every cross-account message.

## Proposal (contributor's, summarised)

- **A `coor` CLI exposed to agents as a skill**, configured by `.env` (channel, broker endpoint, agent id, token):
  - `coor lock <issue|module>`: take a lease;
  - `coor status`: heartbeat, plus current leases;
  - `coor next`: get the highest-priority unleased work order;
  - `coor dispatch`: report a finished unit.
- **A broker on Cloudflare Workers** with Durable Objects holding the lease table and session registry. Leases auto-expire on missed heartbeats, and the broker flags stale branches.
- **GitHub webhooks** feed new issues and PRs to a maintenance/dispatcher agent, which turns them into work orders.
- The original suggests **ZeroMQ compiled to WASM** as the transport.

## Assessment (M5)

**Keep:**
- leases with a heartbeat TTL;
- a small CLI as a skill (works for non-Claude agents too, no MCP server needed);
- a dispatcher (`coor next`);
- webhook ingestion instead of polling.

**Change:**
- **Transport.** Cloudflare Workers can't accept inbound raw TCP (`connect()` is outbound only), so a `tcp://...workers.dev:5555` ZMQ endpoint can't work. One Durable Object per project plus HTTP and WebSocket gives the consistency and notifications without ZMQ or a WASM port.
- **Lease granularity.** Lease the issue and declare the modules it touches, and warn on overlap; don't lock files. The real collisions are on shared hot files (`lib.rs`, `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION`, `assets/posts/*.cps`, `CHANGELOG.md`), and file locks there would serialize everyone. This automates AGENTS.md's "an issue touching code an open PR changes stacks/waits".
- **Unlocks.** Don't rely on SIGINT unlocks. Agent sessions end without clean exits (compaction, API errors, reboots); the heartbeat TTL is the mechanism, and an explicit unlock is a bonus.
- **GitHub stays the record.** The broker mirrors each lease to the existing claim comment and label, so forks, humans and agents outside the system still see it, and nothing breaks if the broker is down.
- **A message channel between agents** (addressed lines, e.g. `@SKULL: #1181 head X ready for re-review`) rides the same broker. That removes the user from the relay loop.

## Open questions

1. **Identity and auth.** One token per agent, issued how? Should agents also get separate GitHub identities (machine users or a GitHub App), since everyone posts as one account today and claims are told apart by text?
2. **Lease scope.** Issue plus declared modules, with an overlap warning or a refusal? How are the "modules it touches" declared, and how are they checked against the PR's actual diff?
3. **Staleness.** The TTL per lease kind (work, review, research), and how it maps onto AGENTS.md's 4 h and 48 h rules. Does the broker replace those rules or only enforce them?
4. **The dispatcher.** Does it only order by P, lanes and effort (deterministic), or is it an agent that also splits issues? Does it know each subscription's remaining budget?
5. **Mirroring to GitHub.** Which token posts the mirror comments, and how are drift or a broker outage reconciled?
6. **Hosting and cost.** Cloudflare free tier (Workers plus Durable Objects) vs. a small VM; who owns the account and its secrets.
7. **The fork case.** How a fork's agents join: the channel is per project, so do fork contributors get read-only or full leases?
8. **The cheaper interim.** A pinned "coordination" issue that every agent reads and posts to each tick, as an hour-long first step. Is it worth doing while this is designed?
9. **Process.** The AGENTS.md changes (claim rules, Pick, lanes) and the PROCESS_VERSION bump once it ships.

## Done means

Every open question above is answered in comments here. The concrete sub-issues are filed: at minimum the broker, the CLI and skill, GitHub mirroring, the webhook ingest, and the AGENTS.md process change. Each carries one `P*`, one `effort:*`, `area:*`, `source:agent`, a "Done means" line and "Part of #<this>". Then this umbrella is closed.

body:
**What happens.** The `PR-reviewer` checks a PR against the laws (unwrap, commands, layering, placement, process) and runs the touched suites, but nothing tells it *where* a behaviour bug is most likely or what to compare the new code with. With a large diff it ends up sampling. And there is no bound on review rounds: a PR can go `needs-rework` -> fix -> full review -> `needs-rework` again, each round on the same (possibly too cheap) worker tier and each round a full review build.

**Evidence.** In another agent-driven Rust project of this contributor, run with the same builder -> reviewer setup, an evaluation on 2026-11-12 found that reviews without named spots took samples and found nothing; the one real finding of the period came only when the dispatcher named the risky places and the reference function to compare with. The same project caps the loop at one rework per tier.

**Proposal (process files only):**
1. `work-issue` step 5: the draft PR body carries a `Risk spots:` list - 3-5 entries, each `file:function - what could go wrong - reference` (the issue's Done means, the public source in the module's provenance line, or the existing function / law the change mirrors). Typical spots: new geometry or formulas, anything that reaches posted G-code, file/project writing and round-trip, state across frames, undo/redo and abort paths.
2. `PR-reviewer` step 5: a new first item "Risk spots, not samples": take the PR's list (or choose 3-5 itself when it is missing), read each hunk and its reference, compare step by step, and name in the review what each spot was compared with.
3. AGENTS.md "Escalation, never silent" and `work-issue` step 4: a PR whose second full review is again `needs-rework` is not reworked a third time on the same tier - the issue's effort label rises one step and the next rework goes to that tier (`max`: `blocked`, maintainer decides).
4. `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` +1.

Suggested labels: `P5`, `effort:low`, `source:agent` (the contributor cannot set labels).

**Done means:** the four files carry the rules above; a fork that syncs to the new PROCESS_VERSION gets them; #681 has the announcement line when it merges.

Part of #290. Found while building #537 (4-axis upper/lower profiles).

**What happens now.** A straight wire cannot touch a twisted (non-developable) ruled surface along its whole height. #537 keeps the kerf out by widening the kerf offset on both profile planes *uniformly* until the leaning kerf stands clear at every height read, and refuses past the op's `four_axis.tolerance`. Two costs follow:

1. The whole profile stands the widening proud of the kerf offset, though only the twisted stretches (e.g. the corners of a square-to-round) need it.
2. The wire laws (`sim::verify::wire`) judge the *mesh* with a 0.1 um tolerance. A model whose tessellation of a twisted wall bulges past the ruled surface between the two picked profiles (any STEP loft tessellated at a chord tolerance) is refused as a gouge - safe, but it blocks a correct cut of a real model.

**Wanted.**
- Widen per ruling (a variable offset along the profiles, with its own corner law) so the standing stock is only where the twist is; the path's note states the worst.
- A stated verify tolerance for a 4-axis cut (the op's own, visible on the report line) against which the wire laws judge the tessellated wall - never silent, never a default that hides a gouge.

Evidence: `crates/motion/src/wire_edm/ruled.rs` (uniform widening), `docs/decisions/537-wire-4axis.md`; the #537 fixture meshes are split along the inner diagonal so they stand inside the ruled surface.

**Done means:** a square-to-round punch stands at the kerf offset on its straight stretches and widened only at the twist (pinned by a motion test reading both), and a lofted model tessellated at a stated chord tolerance posts when the op states a verify tolerance at least that large and is refused by name when it does not (pinned by an app test).

Follow-up of #940 (machining mesh seam, PR stacked on #941).

What #940 delivers: `camcraft_kernel::machining_mesh` refuses by name every `PlanStats` shortfall that touches the guarantee (unmeshed, lenient, unsampled edge, a face or edge capped off its tolerance), pinned by `every_planner_shortfall_is_a_refusal_or_a_note` on SYNTHETIC `PlanStats` values; and a SAMPLED deviation (15 barycentric points a triangle), judged by the closed-form distance to the record's analytic surface where the face is analytic, else by the parametric distance |S(u,v) - T(u,v)|.

Owed:
1. **Real provocations.** No fixture under testdata/models makes the planner report any shortfall (checked at 0.005, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0002 and 0.0001 mm on Milling-test.step and sample_ap214.step). Build small crafted records (a pcurve off its edge, a free edge, a face whose grid must be thinned past `MAX_FACE_GRID`, an edge past 20 000 nodes) and pin that each reaches its named `MeshRefusal` through `machining_mesh`, not only through `judge_stats`.
2. **Spline and revolved faces.** They are judged only by the parametric distance, which over-reads on a non-uniform parameterisation (a few per cent on a rational circle) - a possible false refusal. Add a projection onto the plan surface (Newton from the sample's (u, v)) so they get a true distance, with a fixture that has such a face.
3. **Between the samples.** The deviation is a sampled maximum, a lower bound of the true one; solidcore-tess meshes right up to the tolerance (0.993 of it on Milling-test). Either a stated bound on the sag between samples, or a margin in the seam, so "within" is a guarantee.

What upstream solidcore-tess would need (for the maintainer to raise; not filed upstream): a cancellation hook in `plan`; a per-face measured sag in `PlanStats` for every face; a stated bound on the sag between the planner's sample points.

Everything stays inside `crates/kernel`. Part of #27. Gates #917.

Done means: each shortfall entry is pinned by a crafted record through `machining_mesh`; a non-analytic face is judged by a projected distance with a fixture; the decision file says what bounds the sag between samples.

body:
**What happens**

The 3-2-1 alignment (#187) and `SetWcsOrigin` can set a rotated work offset, and the viewport shows the rotated frame — but nothing downstream machines in it:

- Toolpaths generate in world axes; only the offset's translation (`wcs_context` → `OriginX/Y/Z`) reaches the record stream (`posting_wcs_rotation.rs`).
- Heights / machining planes stay world-Z.
- The post refuses a rotated offset by name (#315, shipped in v0.15.0) — correct and safe, but by then the user has built a state the whole page presented as valid: the display shows a frame the CAM does not machine.

User-reported on main 5fd45923: align a setup's WCS with 3-2-1 on a turned part → the WCS is right in the display, toolpath and machining plane do not follow. Not yet pinned by a test.

**Fix (step 3 of #315, owed)**

Carry the rotation end-to-end, as a user parameter with a default:

- generation and heights compute in the offset's frame, so toolpath and machining planes follow the alignment, and
- the post either bakes rotated coordinates into the program or emits the control's own rotation where the machine declares it (Fanuc G68 / G68.2, Siemens CYCLE800 / ROT, Heidenhain PLANE / CYCL 10 — public control documentation only; a G54 register is translation only on every control).

Interim, if the full carry is not taken at once: the 3-2-1 flow should say at alignment time that a rotated offset will not post (the refusal currently arrives only at the post gate), or steer to part alignment (#330, #746).

**Done means**

A part aligned with a rotated work offset machines in that frame: toolpath, height planes and posted program all carry the same rotation, pinned against a hand-computed program — or the alignment refuses with a clear message before any toolpath exists. Never a display that shows a frame nothing machines.

**Related**: #315 (the shipped refusal), #187 (3-2-1 alignment), #330 / #746 (part alignment, the alternative path), #701 (will create rotated offsets from feature roles and needs this to machine them).

body:
Requested by the maintainer; sibling of #743 (tool and holder bodies as spun profiles).

## Two fixture variants
A fixture is one of:
- **Spun body** (turning: chucks, jaws, collets, faceplates): a half-profile on a centreline, revolved about the spindle axis. The same representation as #743's tool and holder bodies, and the same profile code.
- **Extruded profile** (milling: vises, jaws, parallels, step blocks): a closed 2D profile and an extrusion depth (along a chosen axis), placed in the setup.

## Import paths
- **From DXF.** A spun fixture is a centreline plus a half-profile, like #743. An extruded fixture is a closed profile plus the extrusion depth (entered on import, or from a DXF annotation/layer if present). Editable afterwards the way the half-profile is.
- **From STEP.** Imported as a solid and **kept and saved as STEP** in the fixture library (not converted to a profile): the fixture case keeps the vendor solid. A spun or extruded profile can optionally be derived from it, but the STEP stays the source.
- DXF read/write is shared with #743 (our own, from the published DXF reference: `LINE`, `ARC`, `LWPOLYLINE`, layers), with named refusals for unsupported entities and open or self-crossing profiles.

## Collision and simulation
- Spun and extruded fixtures are meshed for the fixture laws and the simulation from their exact profiles, so a profile edit changes what is checked and drawn.
- A STEP fixture keeps today's mesh path.

## Related
- #743: tool and holder bodies as spun profiles (shares the profile/DXF code).
- #339: handle fixtures and vises (umbrella); #561/#566 (locate the part in a fixture); the fixture library (`fixture_library`, #339); #723 (fixture_library test on Windows).

## Done means
- A spun fixture imports from a DXF half-profile and an extruded fixture from a DXF closed profile plus a depth. Both are tested: the meshed body matches the profile, and malformed input gives a named error, not a panic.
- A STEP fixture imports, saves to the fixture library as STEP, and re-inserts unchanged (test).
- The fixture laws and the simulation use the profile-built bodies (existing fixture suites pass; a new test checks a vise jaw built from a profile is hit by a rapid through it).

title: Process changes - fork maintainers please subscribe

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: P?
labels.description: Paused: never picked until the maintainer sets a real priority

body:
**Subscribe to this issue** (the "Subscribe" button on the right) if you work from a fork of CamCraft, especially with an AI agent.

Forks sync product code only at release tags (AGENTS.md "A fork syncs from upstream at each cut tag"). But the *process* - `AGENTS.md`, the agent definitions in `.claude/agents/`, the skills in `.claude/skills/` and `scripts/gate.*` - changes between releases, and a fork's agents should follow the current rules (review labels, priority labels, release steps, and so on).

**How it works:**
- `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` holds one number. Every PR that changes a process file bumps it.
- Every such PR also adds a comment **here**: the new version, what changed, and what to pull. Subscribers get one notification per change.
- A fork's agent compares its `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` with upstream's at the start of each session and, if upstream is newer, pulls just the process files (AGENTS.md "Process files sync on every session"). Product code still waits for the next release tag.

**To pull by hand:**
```
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/main -- AGENTS.md .claude/agents .claude/skills .claude/PROCESS_VERSION scripts/gate.ps1 scripts/gate.sh
git commit -m "chore(process): sync process files to upstream PROCESS_VERSION <n>"
```

This issue stays open and pinned. It's labelled `P?` so no agent ever picks it up as work.

title: Launch terminal is silent while the app works - add real debug logging (tracing) to stdout

labels.name: enhancement

labels.description: Agent surface and tooling keep up with what shipped

body:
## What happens
When CamCraft is started from a terminal, the terminal tells you almost nothing
about what the app is doing. There is no logging framework in the workspace at
all: no `log` or `tracing` dependency in any Cargo.toml, no subscriber
init in the binaries - just ~185 ad-hoc `println!`/`eprintln!` calls scattered
across crates (cli.rs, gpu_init.rs, shell.rs, the post bin). If a subsystem
decides, refuses, retries, or fails to write a file, no line reaches the
console and the failure is only discovered later by forensics on the output.

## Why now (session of 2026-11-07)
Two incidents this week were diagnosed only by reading source afterwards,
because the console was silent during them:
- **A file did not get saved when post processing** - the post appeared to
  succeed; nothing in the terminal said which path it wrote (or that it wrote
  nothing at all).
- **A limit was hit while generating operations** - the generator aborted on a
  budget/limit; the terminal showed no trace of which cap fired or what the
  result was downgraded to.

Prime Directive says "log diagnostics, never silence" - today we cannot.

## Expected
The launching terminal streams debug-level logs of app activity, filterable:
- project save / post write: source path, destination, bytes, or the reason
  nothing was written;
- operation generation: start, end, duration, which limits/budgets stopped a
  generator and what fallback took over;
- verify/sim refusals: the rule that fired and the numbers behind it;
- commands executing (name + affected entities) at debug level.

## Suggested shape
`tracing` + `tracing_subscriber` fmt layer writing to stderr at startup of the
UI binary, default level `info`, overridable by `RUST_LOG` (or a camcraft
config/env of our own). Instrument the command dispatch seam, generators, and
post entry points - the crates are already split (M4.1), so each takes its own
span targets (`camcraft_app::post`, `camcraft_motion::adaptive`, ...). Keep
hot generation loops behind level gates - logging must not slow generation.

## Done means
- Launching the app and running a post writes terminal lines naming the file
  path and result; a failed/skipped write says why.
- Hitting a generation budget (e.g. an Adaptive limit) prints which limit and
  what happened next.
- Levels are controlled by env var, default output stays quiet at `info`, and
  the batch gate shows no measurable generation slowdown.

Found while debugging the post-save incident (user request, 2026-11-07).
